title: The ninth Guru's voice
hookLine: his hymns are short, calm and plain, about the passing world and the steady Name

lines: THE QUIET MAN WHO MADE NO CLAIM.
cards: Sikh tradition tells this story. The boy Guru, Har Krishan, was dying in Delhi, and said only that the next Guru would be found at Bakala, a village in Punjab. Soon Bakala was full of men claiming to be Guru.
Then a trader named Makhan Shah arrived. Caught in a storm at sea, he had vowed five hundred gold coins to the Guru if his ship survived. It had.
So he went from claimant to claimant, laying two coins before each. Each one took them, pleased. At last he found a quiet man who had made no claim at all.
That man looked up and asked about the rest of the promise.

teach.h: THE QUIET MAN BECAME THE NINTH GURU.
teach.b: Tradition says Makhan Shah ran up to the rooftop shouting that he had found the Guru. The quiet man was Tegh Bahadur, youngest son of Guru Hargobind, and he became the ninth Guru.
Tradition remembers long years he had spent at Bakala in meditation, and that stillness is all over his hymns. Sikh tradition says his bani was added to the Granth by his son, Guru Gobind Singh.

teach.h: SHABADS AND SALOKS, ADDED BY HIS SON.
teach.b: It's a short body of work next to Guru Arjan's: shabads spread through the ragas, and a run of saloks near the very end of the book.
Some readers hear his language leaning toward Braj, the old poetic speech of the region around Mathura, softer and more flowing than the Punjabi of the earlier Gurus. The hymns are short.
They often speak straight to someone: saadho, holy ones, or man re, O mind. And they keep returning to two things.
Everything you see is passing, like a dream or the shadow of a cloud. And the Name of the Lord is the one thing that stays. No anger, no fireworks.

Just plain, calm sentences, the way an older friend talks to you when it matters. Sikhs remember that he gave his life in Delhi, refusing to bow under force, and his hymns are the voice of the man who walked toward that.
For the next month, it's the voice in your ears: one that doesn't raise itself, and is very hard to forget.

how: Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabads, marked Mahalla 9, are sung in kirtan across many ragas, and his saloks are read near the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

games.q: you're Makhan Shah. you vowed five hundred gold coins to the Guru, and Bakala is full of claimants. what do you do?
o: give all five hundred to the first claimant you meet.
lay two coins before each and wait.
go home and keep the gold.
games.why: tradition says he laid two coins before each. only the quiet man who made no claim asked about the rest of the vow, and Makhan Shah shouted from the rooftop that he had found the Guru.

practice: Find a recording of a shabad by Guru Tegh Bahadur, marked Mahalla nine, and play it with your eyes closed, listening to its pace and plainness rather than working at the meaning.
If you can't play anything, sit quietly and imagine a voice that never hurries, saying something true, and notice what your breath does when nothing is shouting at it.
